Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 97, verse 1–5:

(p-311) Sūrat al-Qadr (The Night of Decree)

It is Meccan according to the majority, and Medinan according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk. al-Wāqidī mentioned that it was the first surah to be revealed in Medina.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾, has two interpretations.

The first: "it" refers to Jibrīl, meaning that God sent him down during the Night of Decree with the revelation he brought.

The second: "it" refers to the Qur'an, and on this there are two views:

The first is what Ibn ʿAbbās narrated, who said: The Qur'an was sent down in Ramaḍān, during the Night of Decree, on a blessed night, all at once from God the Exalted, from the Preserved Tablet to the noble scribe-angels (al-safara al-kiram al-katibin) in the lowest heaven. The scribe-angels then revealed it to Jibrīl in portions over twenty nights, and Jibrīl revealed it to the Prophet ﷺ over twenty years, descending at the places of the stars (mawaqi al-nujum) in installments (arsalan), in months and days.(p-312)

The second view: that God the Exalted began sending it down during the Night of Decree. This was said by al-Shaʿbī.

There is disagreement about the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr), although they agree that it is within the last ten nights of Ramaḍān, and that it is more likely to be on an odd night of those ten. The exception is Ibn ʿUmar, who claimed that it is in the whole month.

al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, held that it is on the twenty-first or the twenty-third, on the basis of the ḥadīth of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbās held that it is on the night of the twenty-seventh.

There is disagreement about the evidence. Ubayy argued that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Among its signs is that the sun rises in the morning without its rays," and he said: "I saw that on the morning of the twenty-seventh." Ibn ʿAbbās argued that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Sūrat al-Qadr has thirty words," so the word "salām" and the word "hiya" form the twenty-seventh word, which indicates that it is in that night.

Others said: it is on the night of the twenty-fourth, based on the report transmitted concerning the revelation of the scrolls (tanzil al-suhuf). Others said: God the Exalted moves it every year from one night to another, so that people strive throughout all ten nights and look forward to witnessing it.

As for naming it "the Night of Decree" (laylat al-qadr), there are four aspects:

The first: because God the Exalted decreed (qaddara) in it the sending down of the Qur'an.

The second: because God the Exalted determines in it the affairs of the year, that is, He decides them, which is the meaning of Mujāhid's statement.

The third: because of its great worth (ʿiẓam qadriha) and the grandeur of its status, from the expression "a man who has qadr" ("rajul lahu qadr"), mentioned by Ibn ʿĪsā.

The fourth: because acts of obedience have great worth (qadr ʿaẓīm) and abundant reward in it.

﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ as a reminder to the Messenger of God ﷺ of its excellence and as an encouragement to act in it. al-Shaʿbī said: Its night is like its day, and its day like its night.(p-313)

al-Farrāʾ said: Everything in the Qur'an of the form "wa mā adrāka" (and what will make you know) — He has made him know it; and what is of the form "wa mā yudrīka" (and what can make you know) — He has not made him know it.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: God decrees in the Night of Decree only happiness and blessings, and decrees in other nights afflictions and punishments. ʿIkrima said: Ibn ʿAbbās used to call the Night of Decree "the Night of Glorification" (laylat al-taʿẓīm), the midnight of Shaʿbān "the Night of Acquittal" (laylat al-barāʾa), and the two nights of the two ʿIds "the Night of Reward" (laylat al-jāʾiza).

﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾. On this there are six views:

The first: the Night of Decree is better than a lifetime of a thousand months. This was said by al-Rabīʿ.

The second: that acting during the Night of Decree is better than acting during other nights for a thousand months. This was said by Mujāhid.

The third: that the Night of Decree is better than a thousand months which do not include the Night of Decree. This was said by Qatāda.

The fourth: that there was a man among the Children of Israel who would stand in prayer through the night until morning, then fight the enemy until evening, and he did this for a thousand months. God the Exalted then informed that standing in prayer during the Night of Decree is better than that man's deeds for a thousand months. This was narrated by Ibn Abī Najīḥ and Mujāhid.

The fifth: that the kingdom of Sulaymān lasted five hundred months and the kingdom of Dhū al-Qarnayn lasted five hundred months, so their kingdoms together came to a thousand months, and He made acting during the Night of Decree better than the period of their rule.

﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾. Abū Hurayra said: The angels on earth during the Night of Decree are more numerous than the number of pebbles.

As for "al-Rūḥ" (the Spirit) here, there are four views: The first: Jibrīl, peace be upon him. This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: the guardian angels (ḥafaẓat al-malāʾika). This was said by Ibn Abī Najīḥ.

The third: that they are the most noble of the angels and the closest to God. This was said by Muqātil.

The fourth: that they are an army of God other than the angels, narrated by Mujāhid from Ibn ʿAbbās with a raised (marfūʿ) attribution.(p-314)

It is possible, if no explicit text is established on it, that there is a fifth view: that the Spirit and mercy descend with the angels upon its people. The evidence is the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾, meaning with mercy.

﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾, meaning by the command of their Lord.

﴿For every matter﴾, meaning: what is decreed in that night of provision and term until its like in the coming year.

Ibn ʿAbbās read "min kulli imriʾ" (for every person). al-Kalbī interpreted it as meaning that Jibrīl descends in it with the angels, and they greet every believing person.

﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾. On this there are three interpretations: The first: that the Night of Decree is a night safe from every evil; no harm occurs in it and no devil is sent forth in it. This was said by Mujāhid.

The second: that the Night of Decree is peace, goodness and blessing. This was said by Qatāda.

The third: that the angels greet the believers during the Night of Decree until the emergence of dawn. This was said by al-Kalbī.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 97, verse 1–5:

(p-311) Sūrat al-Qadr (The Night of Decree)

It is Meccan according to the majority, and Medinan according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk. al-Wāqidī mentioned that it was the first surah to be revealed in Medina.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾, has two interpretations.

The first: "it" refers to Jibrīl, meaning that God sent him down during the Night of Decree with the revelation he brought.

The second: "it" refers to the Qur'an, and on this there are two views:

The first is what Ibn ʿAbbās narrated, who said: The Qur'an was sent down in Ramaḍān, during the Night of Decree, on a blessed night, all at once from God the Exalted, from the Preserved Tablet to the noble scribe-angels (al-safara al-kiram al-katibin) in the lowest heaven. The scribe-angels then revealed it to Jibrīl in portions over twenty nights, and Jibrīl revealed it to the Prophet ﷺ over twenty years, descending at the places of the stars (mawaqi al-nujum) in installments (arsalan), in months and days.(p-312)

The second view: that God the Exalted began sending it down during the Night of Decree. This was said by al-Shaʿbī.

There is disagreement about the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr), although they agree that it is within the last ten nights of Ramaḍān, and that it is more likely to be on an odd night of those ten. The exception is Ibn ʿUmar, who claimed that it is in the whole month.

al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, held that it is on the twenty-first or the twenty-third, on the basis of the ḥadīth of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbās held that it is on the night of the twenty-seventh.

There is disagreement about the evidence. Ubayy argued that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Among its signs is that the sun rises in the morning without its rays," and he said: "I saw that on the morning of the twenty-seventh." Ibn ʿAbbās argued that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Sūrat al-Qadr has thirty words," so the word "salām" and the word "hiya" form the twenty-seventh word, which indicates that it is in that night.

Others said: it is on the night of the twenty-fourth, based on the report transmitted concerning the revelation of the scrolls (tanzil al-suhuf). Others said: God the Exalted moves it every year from one night to another, so that people strive throughout all ten nights and look forward to witnessing it.

As for naming it "the Night of Decree" (laylat al-qadr), there are four aspects:

The first: because God the Exalted decreed (qaddara) in it the sending down of the Qur'an.

The second: because God the Exalted determines in it the affairs of the year, that is, He decides them, which is the meaning of Mujāhid's statement.

The third: because of its great worth (ʿiẓam qadriha) and the grandeur of its status, from the expression "a man who has qadr" ("rajul lahu qadr"), mentioned by Ibn ʿĪsā.

The fourth: because acts of obedience have great worth (qadr ʿaẓīm) and abundant reward in it.

﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ as a reminder to the Messenger of God ﷺ of its excellence and as an encouragement to act in it. al-Shaʿbī said: Its night is like its day, and its day like its night.(p-313)

al-Farrāʾ said: Everything in the Qur'an of the form "wa mā adrāka" (and what will make you know) — He has made him know it; and what is of the form "wa mā yudrīka" (and what can make you know) — He has not made him know it.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: God decrees in the Night of Decree only happiness and blessings, and decrees in other nights afflictions and punishments. ʿIkrima said: Ibn ʿAbbās used to call the Night of Decree "the Night of Glorification" (laylat al-taʿẓīm), the midnight of Shaʿbān "the Night of Acquittal" (laylat al-barāʾa), and the two nights of the two ʿIds "the Night of Reward" (laylat al-jāʾiza).

﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾. On this there are six views:

The first: the Night of Decree is better than a lifetime of a thousand months. This was said by al-Rabīʿ.

The second: that acting during the Night of Decree is better than acting during other nights for a thousand months. This was said by Mujāhid.

The third: that the Night of Decree is better than a thousand months which do not include the Night of Decree. This was said by Qatāda.

The fourth: that there was a man among the Children of Israel who would stand in prayer through the night until morning, then fight the enemy until evening, and he did this for a thousand months. God the Exalted then informed that standing in prayer during the Night of Decree is better than that man's deeds for a thousand months. This was narrated by Ibn Abī Najīḥ and Mujāhid.

The fifth: that the kingdom of Sulaymān lasted five hundred months and the kingdom of Dhū al-Qarnayn lasted five hundred months, so their kingdoms together came to a thousand months, and He made acting during the Night of Decree better than the period of their rule.

﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾. Abū Hurayra said: The angels on earth during the Night of Decree are more numerous than the number of pebbles.

As for "al-Rūḥ" (the Spirit) here, there are four views: The first: Jibrīl, peace be upon him. This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: the guardian angels (ḥafaẓat al-malāʾika). This was said by Ibn Abī Najīḥ.

The third: that they are the most noble of the angels and the closest to God. This was said by Muqātil.

The fourth: that they are an army of God other than the angels, narrated by Mujāhid from Ibn ʿAbbās with a raised (marfūʿ) attribution.(p-314)

It is possible, if no explicit text is established on it, that there is a fifth view: that the Spirit and mercy descend with the angels upon its people. The evidence is the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾, meaning with mercy.

﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾, meaning by the command of their Lord.

﴿For every matter﴾, meaning: what is decreed in that night of provision and term until its like in the coming year.

Ibn ʿAbbās read "min kulli imriʾ" (for every person). al-Kalbī interpreted it as meaning that Jibrīl descends in it with the angels, and they greet every believing person.

﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾. On this there are three interpretations: The first: that the Night of Decree is a night safe from every evil; no harm occurs in it and no devil is sent forth in it. This was said by Mujāhid.

The second: that the Night of Decree is peace, goodness and blessing. This was said by Qatāda.

The third: that the angels greet the believers during the Night of Decree until the emergence of dawn. This was said by al-Kalbī.
